terms.comment: Latin puts “forward” into the verb with prō-: prōcēdere, step forward (illūc prōcēde, Plaut. Capt., Lewis & Short), prōgredī, go forward; and prōnus is “leaning forward” (Lewis & Short).

evidence: de Vaan 481, s.v. por-: “straight on, forward, further”
terms.comment: With verbs of going on, also of going on with a story: perge porrō, carry on.

evidence: Ter. Hec. 315: cursārī rūrsum prōrsum, “running back and forth”
terms.comment: Mostly in comedy; rūrsum prōrsum is “back and forth”.

phrases.latin: Quam tarda es! inquit; nōn vīs citius prōgredī?
phrases.english: “How slow you are!” he said. “Won’t you get a move on?”

phrases.latin: pergeret porrō īre nec ultrā inquīreret
phrases.english: he was to keep going forward and ask no further

phrases.latin: Trepidārī sentiō et cursārī rūrsum prōrsum.
phrases.english: I can hear people bustling and running back and forth.

sources: Lewis & Short: progredior · Lewis & Short: procedo · Lewis & Short: porro · Lewis & Short: prorsum
Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 481.
